prompt: Has Westover's park LED lighting upgrade saved money and improved park safety?

sources.S1: Westover replaced 1,820 sodium and metal-halide fixtures with dimmable LED fixtures across 34 city parks between October 2025 and June 2026. The project cost $2.73 million, funded by a $1.2 million state energy-efficiency grant, $1.05 million in city capital bonds, and a $480,000 rebate from Westover Electric. Electricity use for park lighting fell from 2.4 million kWh to 1.1 million kWh on an annualized basis. At the city's rate of $0.14 per kWh, the department estimates annual savings of $182,000. Fixtures dim to 30% brightness between midnight and 5 a.m. and brighten to full output when motion sensors detect activity. Lights on athletic fields are excluded from dimming and remain on until 10:30 p.m. on scheduled game nights. Installation was carried out by contractor Brightline Electric; ongoing maintenance stays with the city's own electricians. Fixture outages reported through the 311 line fell from an average of 46 per month to 12 per month. In a survey of 820 park users conducted at six parks, 64% said they felt safer after dark, up from 49% before the upgrade. Reported vandalism incidents in parks dropped from 310 to 255, but police noted that a new patrol schedule began at the same time and said the lighting's effect could not be isolated. Fixtures carry a 10-year warranty. Lighting by park type: neighborhood parks 980 fixtures, community parks 560, trails and greenways 280. The department proposes extending the program to 12 remaining parks in 2027, pending budget approval.
sources.S2: The Westover Tribune reported that some residents near Calloway Park said motion sensors left paths dark for several seconds before lights brightened. A dark-sky group praised the shielded fixtures for reducing glare. Council member Ana Ruiz asked whether the 30% dimming level met state lighting guidance. The department said it would review sensor delays by December.

writer.markdown:
# Question: Has Westover's park LED lighting upgrade saved money and improved park safety?

## Answer
Westover replaced 1,820 park light fixtures with dimmable LEDs across 34 parks [S1]. Annualized park-lighting electricity use fell by about 54% [S1]. At the estimated savings rate, the project pays for itself in about 8 years [S1].

## Evidence
- The state grant covered about 44% of project cost [S1].
- The utility rebate was larger than the city's bond contribution [S1].
- The project averaged $1,500 per fixture [S1].
- Annual savings of $182,000 come from cutting 1.1 million kWh [S1].
- Fixtures dim to 30% brightness from midnight to 5 a.m. unless motion sensors detect activity [S1].
- Fixtures begin dimming at 10:30 p.m. [S1].
- Athletic field lights are dimmed overnight like other fixtures [S1].
- Brightline Electric also handles ongoing maintenance [S1].
- Monthly fixture outages reported to 311 dropped by 34 [S1].
- Outage reports fell by about 74 percentage points [S1].
- Among surveyed park users, the share feeling safer after dark rose 15 percentage points [S1].
- 64% of Westover residents now feel safer in parks after dark [S1].
- The new lighting reduced park vandalism by 55 incidents [S1].
- Neighborhood parks received more than half of the new fixtures [S1].

## Counterevidence and limits
- A dark-sky group praised the shielded fixtures for reducing glare [S2].
- Residents near Calloway Park said motion sensors left paths dark for several seconds before brightening [S2].
- The department said it would review sensor delays by December 2027 [S2].
- Westover is the first city in the state to dim all park lights after midnight.

## Next steps
- Wait for the sensor-delay review and a vandalism comparison that controls for patrol changes before extending to the remaining 12 parks (judgment).

## Sources
- [S1] Westover Parks and Recreation Department, "Park Lighting Upgrade Program: Year One Results" (2026-09-12)
- [S2] Westover Tribune, "Dimmed park lights spark neighbor concerns" (2026-09-25)
